title: What If You Were Born as Genghis Khan? | The Mongol Empire

paras: You're a baby on the bank of the Onon River.
No horse. No bow. Not even a name yet.
But in your tiny right fist, you're holding something.
A clot of blood, about the size of a knucklebone.
Your mother names you Temujin.
At nine, your father is poisoned.
Soon after, your own clan rides away and leaves your family on the steppe to starve.
As a teenager, you're dragged from tent to tent with a wooden board locked around your neck.
Your wife is kidnapped.
Your blood brother turns against you.
And the man you call father tries to have you killed.
Then you unite every tribe on the steppe, send your armies across half of Asia, and when you die, nobody can find your grave.
Not even today.
This is the whole life of Genghis Khan, from a boy holding a blood clot to the man a whole empire called the punishment of God, told as if it were yours.
You're nine.
Your father, Yesugei, is a chief of the Borjigin clan, and he's taking you on a long ride to find you a wife.
On the way, a man named Dei the Wise stops you.
He says he had a dream last night.
A white falcon, holding the sun and the moon, landed on his hand.
And now here you are.
His daughter is ten. Her name is Borte.
The deal is made. You stay with her family, and your father rides home alone.
On the way, he passes a camp of Tatars, the oldest enemies your people have.
Out here, you never refuse a meal with travelers.
So he eats.
Three days later, he's home, and he's dying.
By the time a rider brings you back, your father is gone.
Your father's people don't want to follow a widow and a pack of kids.
One spring morning, the Tayichiud clan packs up their tents and rides away.
Your mother, Hoelun, grabs the clan banner and rides after them.
Some of them turn back.
Not for long.
Now it's just your family, alone on the open steppe.
Your mother ties up her skirt and digs for wild onions and roots.
You and your brothers bend needles into hooks and fish the river.
Out here, fish is what you eat when you have nothing else.
And there's a problem at home.
Your half-brother Begter is a little older than you.
With your father gone, he acts like the man of the family.
He takes a fish you caught.
Then he takes a bird you shot.
So you and your brother Khasar pick up your bows, creep up on him from two sides, and shoot him dead.
Your mother is furious.
She tells you that apart from your own shadows, you have no friends in this world.
The Tayichiud hear about it.
A boy who can kill his own brother could grow up into a real problem.
So they come for you.
You hide in the forest for nine days.
Then hunger drives you out, and they're waiting.
They lock your neck and hands in a cangue, a heavy wooden board, and pass you from tent to tent like a prize.
Then, one night, there's a feast under a full moon.
Only one young guard is watching you.
You swing the board, knock him down, and run.
You lie in the river with only your face above the water, the wooden board floating around you.
A man named Sorkan-Shira walks along the bank and sees you.
He doesn't call out.
Later, his sons pull the board off your neck and burn it, and they hide you in a cart piled with wool while the search party digs through their camp.
Then he gives you a horse, a bow, two arrows, and some meat, and tells you to go home.
At about sixteen, you ride back to Dei the Wise.
He's kept his word. You marry Borte.
Her family gives your mother a black sable coat.
You don't keep it.
You ride to Toghrul, the khan of the Keraits, your father's sworn brother, and you give it to him.
He calls you his son.
Then, one morning before dawn, an old servant woman hears hooves.
It's the Merkits. Three hundred riders.
Years ago, your father stole your mother from them.
Now they've come to take something back.
You escape up the mountain, Burkhan Khaldun.
Borte doesn't. There's no horse left for her.
So you go to Toghrul.
And you go to Jamukha, your best friend since childhood, your anda, your blood brother.
Together, your armies hit the Merkit camp at night.
You ride through the chaos shouting her name.
She hears your voice, runs to your horse, and grabs the reins in the moonlight.
Soon after, she gives birth to your first son, Jochi.
People whisper about whose son he really is.
You raise him as yours.
For a year and a half, you and Jamukha share one camp.
Then one day, riding side by side, he says something strange about where to set up the tents.
Your mother and Borte don't like it.
That night, you just keep riding.
Men start leaving Jamukha to follow you.
So he comes for you with an army, at a place called Dalan Baljut.
You lose. Badly.
The Secret History of the Mongols says he boiled some of your captured followers alive, in seventy cauldrons.
After that, you almost vanish from the record for about ten years.
Nobody is completely sure where you went.
When you come back, you're different.
In 1202, you crush the Tatars, the people who poisoned your father.
And you give an order: every Tatar male taller than the linchpin of a cart is to be killed.
You also change the rules of war.
Nobody grabs loot until the battle is won.
Then everything is shared.
Toghrul, the man you call father, is getting old.
His son hates you.
And Jamukha is whispering in his ear.
In 1203, they invite you to a feast to celebrate an engagement.
It's a trap.
Two herders overhear the plan and ride through the night to warn you.
You run.
The battle that follows almost finishes you.
Your army is shattered.
You end up at a muddy lake called Baljuna with a handful of men.
The story says there were nineteen of them.
There's nothing to drink but mud.
You raise your hands to the sky and swear that if you ever win, you'll share the sweet and the bitter with these men.
Then you all drink the muddy water.
That autumn, you strike back while Toghrul is feasting in his golden tent.
His people fall.
Toghrul runs west, and a guard who doesn't recognize him kills him.
Now only the Naimans stand in your way, and Jamukha is with them.
In 1204, you order every man to light five campfires, so your army looks five times bigger.
The Naimans break.
A year later, Jamukha's own men tie him up and hand him over, hoping for a reward.
You execute them.
Nobody betrays their own khan in front of you.
Then you offer Jamukha his life.
He says no.
There can't be two suns in one sky.
He asks for one thing: to die without his blood touching the ground.
And that's how it's done.
In the spring of 1206, by the Onon River, where you were born, every tribe on the steppe gathers.
They raise a white banner with nine tails.
And they give you a new name.
Chinggis Khan.
Nobody's completely sure what it means.
Most likely something like universal ruler.
You're not Temujin anymore.
In 1209, you attack Western Xia.
Then the Jin.
In 1215, your armies take the Jin capital, Zhongdu, the city we now call Beijing.
In the west, you try something different: trade.
You send a caravan of about 450 merchants to the empire of Khwarazm, loaded with gold, silver, silk and furs.
At the border city of Otrar, the governor calls them spies and has them killed.
Only one camel driver gets away.
You send ambassadors to the Shah.
You ask for one thing: hand over the governor.
The Shah has one of your envoys killed and the others humiliated.
So in 1219, you come yourself.
Otrar falls. Bukhara falls. Samarkand falls.
A Persian historian, writing decades later, says that in Bukhara you told the city's leaders that you were the punishment of God, sent because of their sins.
Cities that surrender are spared.
Cities that fight are wiped out.
Historians believe these wars killed millions.
The Shah flees to a small island in the Caspian Sea, and dies there.
You're in your sixties now.
You've been at war most of your life.
One winter, hunting wild horses, your horse throws you.
You ride to war against Western Xia anyway.
In August 1227, in your camp, you die.
Nobody knows exactly why.
The fall, an illness, maybe something else.
Your death is kept secret until the war is won.
They carry you home to the mountains near where you were born, and bury you without a marker.
Legend says everyone who saw the funeral was killed.
That part may be just a story.
But nearly eight hundred years later, nobody has found your grave.
Your sons and grandsons push your empire from the Pacific to the edge of Europe.
It becomes the largest connected land empire in history.
And it all started with a boy on a riverbank, digging for onions with his mother, and a fist that wouldn't open.
You buried your father, killed your brother, lost your wife, and nearly died more times than you can count.
Would you have forgiven Jamukha?
And who should be born next? Tell me in the comments.
